summary: This informational document gives a framework for setting up and controlling MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineered label switched paths across multiple domains, where a domain is any set of network elements under common address management or path computation responsibility, such as an IGP area or an autonomous system.

plainLanguage.summary: Planning a delivery route across several countries means coordinating many rulebooks. This lays out how to plan reserved routes that cross such borders.

questions: what is inter-domain mpls traffic engineering
what is a path computation element
how are te lsps set up across multiple domains
subtitle: A map of the signaling, path computation and information-sharing options for traffic-engineered MPLS paths that cross domain borders.

tldr.problem: Traffic-engineered label switched paths are easy to set up inside one routing area or AS, but real networks often need them to cross several domains that do not share topology or address management.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits the problem into three parts: signaling (nesting, contiguous or stitched LSPs), path computation (at the ingress, at domain borders, or by a Path Computation Element), and distribution of reachability and TE information.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework only: it names the options and their trade-offs, and leaves protocol details and choices between techniques to other documents and applicability statements.

today: RFC 4726 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a framework and defines no protocol, and it relies on related RFCs such as RFC 4655 for path computation elements.

sections.title: Scope and Definition of a Domain
sections.content:
This RFC gives a framework for establishing and controlling MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineered (TE) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in multi-domain networks. It builds on requirements for inter-area and inter-AS MPLS traffic engineering set out in RFC 4105 and RFC 4216.

A domain is any collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computational responsibility. IGP areas and Autonomous Systems are the examples given. Wholly or partially overlapping domains, and nested domains, are outside the scope.

The RFC separates the functional pieces into discovering reachability and TE information, computing LSP paths, and signaling the LSPs. It does not detail each technique; those are covered in other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain is like one country's road system, run by one authority. The document is about building a special reserved lane that passes through several countries.

sections.title: Signaling Options
sections.content:
Three ways to signal a TE LSP across domains are identified. The right choice may depend on the path computation technique, the application, and the nature of the network. Comparing them is left to a separate applicability statement.

  • LSP nesting: one TE LSP is carried inside a hierarchical LSP. The hierarchical LSP can carry many nested LSPs along a common part of their paths, or just one. A hierarchical LSP that spans multiple domains cannot be advertised as a TE link.
  • Contiguous LSP: a single LSP is set up from ingress to egress in one signaling exchange, using the same Session/LSP ID at every LSR.
  • LSP stitching: separate LSP segments, each signaled as a distinct TE LSP with its own source and destination, are joined in the data plane into one end-to-end LSP.

Methods can be mixed in a single inter-domain LSP, and the choice may be reported along the path, for example through the Record Route Object. An ingress that wants to restrict which methods are used downstream could do so with new flags, but the RFC says the need must first be established and compatibility considered.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ride one big bus that carries smaller buses, take one long trip without changing, or change vehicles at each border. Each way gets you across.

sections.title: Path Computation Techniques
sections.content:
The RFC limits itself to where computation happens and how much of the path is worked out, not to the algorithms. Techniques are tied to signaling methods, so some pairings are required.

  • Management configuration: an offline tool or planner supplies the path, which the ingress encodes as an Explicit Route Object (ERO).
  • Head-end computation: with multi-domain visibility the ingress computes the whole path. With partial visibility it supplies explicit hops to its domain boundary plus loose hops or abstract nodes for the other domains. With local visibility only, it supplies explicit hops to the boundary and a loose hop for the egress.
  • Domain boundary computation: the LSR at each boundary adds enough path information to reach the next boundary. These computations are independent, so path quality can be unpredictable to the ingress, and paths may loop back into a domain already crossed.
  • Path Computation Element (PCE): an LSR may hand computation to a PCE. A PCE can give a full path, or only a partial one to preserve topology confidentiality, or there can be one per domain.

No single definition of an optimal path is given. The RFC notes that it is impossible to guarantee optimal routing when routing information is aggregated, abstracted or summarized.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone has to draw the map of the route. The first driver might draw all of it, or just the first leg, and each border guard draws the next leg, or a helper office draws it for everyone.

sections.title: Distributing Information and Advanced Functions
sections.content:
Path computation works on a TE Database filled with reachability and TE information. Inside a domain this information is distributed by IGP extensions such as RFC 3630 and RFC 3784. For links that join two domains, the RFC says there should be a mechanism to give each side the TE information about them, which would improve path computation and reduce crankbacks. Before new protocol work on cross-domain advertisement begins, the RFC says requirements and benefits must be clearly established, and that has not been done to date.

The RFC also comments on how inter-domain operation affects other functions:

  • Re-optimization and repair: moving or fixing an LSP may involve several domains, and mutually diverse paths must be known together.
  • Setup failure: retry within the failing domain first, then report back upstream, which conflicts with topology confidentiality.
  • Fast Reroute: the failure cases include a domain edge node present in both domains, one present in only one, and an inter-domain link. Fast Reroute applies only to packet networks.
  • Other topics: domain-specific meaning of constraints, policy control at boundaries, OAM, and non-packet technologies. Point-to-multipoint is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Border crossings need to share some traffic news so planners pick good routes, but not too much. If a road breaks in the middle of the trip, there are rules for who tries to fix it first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Inside a domain, security requirements are unchanged from the existing MPLS signaling and routing protocols. Across domains the issue is more sensitive, because control and information pass over administrative boundaries; inter-AS TE is the most sensitive case. The RFC says a separate document must analyze the deployment models and risks before inter-domain MPLS TE solution documents can advance.

One new concept appears: preservation of topology confidentiality. A domain may want to keep secret how its network is built and what resources are free. Policy filters must then be applied at domain boundaries, and the distributing domain is responsible for this. Coordination of keys or passwords across administrative domains will need human-to-human coordination at this stage.
sections.plainLanguage: A country may not want to show foreign planners its whole road map. So the border keeps some details secret, and the countries must agree on passwords in person.
